name: HIAS: programmes for refugees abroad
beneficiaries_note: Our build: HIAS's country programmes, weighted by the people each served in 2025 (Form 990 Schedule O: Chad 257,700, Colombia 36,700, Ukraine and Moldova 32,300, Panama 23,000, Ecuador about 21,000, Costa Rica 6,700) and smaller programmes in Mexico, Venezuela, Kenya, Israel and Greece; a judgment, as HIAS publishes no spending by country.
summary: HIAS spent $48.1 million in the year to September 2025 on programmes for refugees and displaced people in about 15 countries, the largest for Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad and for Venezuelans and others across Latin America: cash and basic needs for 54,000 people, legal protection for 81,000, violence prevention and support for 80,500, mental-health support for 73,100 and economic inclusion for 6,000 (calendar 2025 counts). Each activity is built from the research on that kind of work: cash and goods on the site's log-income scale (with a few crisis deaths averted), legal status from Colombia's regularisation natural experiment, mental-health and survivors' support in life satisfaction from humanitarian trials, and economic inclusion from the graduation trials. It comes to about 0.05 years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.01-0.2), below the site's global-health median and near Samaritan's Purse and the Red Cross's international work, because much of the spending is on protection and legal work whose measurable gains are small per person. Every branch is discounted for missing data: HIAS counts the people reached but publishes no controlled measure of its own results; the biggest uncertainties are that discount, displaced people's consumption and the share of spending that reaches people as cash.

sections.explainer: What the modelled programme cost in fiscal 2025 (October 2024 to September 2025), with its share of management and fundraising, from HIAS's audited consolidated accounts. Donated legal services, booked in the accounts at the law firms' rates, are not HIAS's own money: they enter the credit share, not the cost.

sections.title: Effect per person
sections.explainer: What the help does for each person reached, from the research on that kind of work, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, delivery falling short and missing outcome data. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction) and put into healthy years by its unit's conversion, so each moves only with its own sliders.

sections.title: Your dollar's share

rows.label: Share of the people served in Africa (Chad, Kenya, South Africa)
rows.explainer: Chad alone served 257,700 people of HIAS's 544,000 to 567,000 (Form 990 Schedule O), most of them through camp-wide services; the branches' counts lean less on Chad. 45% (30-60%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of the people served in Europe and Israel (Ukraine, Moldova, Greece, Israel)
rows.explainer: 32,300 in Ukraine and Moldova, 1,100 in Israel (Form 990 Schedule O): 12% (5-20%). Our judgment.

rows.formula: africa_share * avg(cons_ken, cons_uga) + europe_share * cons_ukr + (1 - africa_share - europe_share) * avg(cons_hnd, cons_per)
rows.explainer: Kenya and Uganda stand in for Chad and Kenya (the site has no survey figure for Chad, poorer than both); Honduras and Peru for Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Mexico and Venezuela; Ukraine for Ukraine and Moldova.

rows.label: Displaced people's consumption as a share of the average
rows.explainer: Refugees in camps in eastern Chad and Venezuelans in transit consume far below their hosts; settled refugees in cities less so. 45% (30-70%), as in the site's other relief models. Our judgment.

rows.label: Displaced people's consumption per person (2024 US dollars)

rows.label: Death rate of the people given cash and basic needs (per person-year)
rows.explainer: Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad's camps, where surveys found crude death rates around the emergency threshold, and migrants crossing the Darién; most cash goes to settled Venezuelans and refugees in towns, near their hosts' rates. 1% a year (0.7-2%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Normal death rate (per person-year)
rows.explainer: The site's Sudan figure (UN World Population Prospects), the rate the refugees would face at home in peace.

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths averted for the people reached
rows.explainer: Cash and food lower crisis mortality modestly where people go hungry; most recipients aren't at that edge. 3% (0-10%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years of the crisis the help covers
rows.explainer: One to six months of transfers. A quarter of a year (0.1-0.5). Our judgment.

Share of the deaths averted under five

rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Illness averted per person given cash and basic needs (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Clean water (4,200 people in Venezuela) and food avert some diarrhoea and malnutrition: a small amount. Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of the mental-health count given structured support (counselling, groups)
rows.explainer: The count includes people reached through awareness sessions and trained community members; HIAS served 13,000 in Chad with services and over 900 in Kenya directly (Form 990 Schedule O). 30% (15-50%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Effect of the support on distress, in standard deviations
rows.explainer: WHO's low-intensity psychological interventions for people exposed to adversity reduce distress by 0.45 SD (0.34-0.56) across 23 trials (Schäfer et al. 2023, World Psychiatry, https://doi.org/10.1002/wps.21129); HIAS's community-based psychosocial support is less structured than the trials' programmes: 0.3 SD (0.15-0.5). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years the effect lasts
rows.explainer: Follow-ups of brief psychological interventions show effects fading over one to two years: a year at full effect (0.5-2), as in the site's other humanitarian models. Our judgment.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person counted, discounted
rows.explainer: SD-years × the site's WELLBYs per SD-year, over the whole count.

rows.label: Share of the violence count given direct support (case management, safe spaces, survivors' care)
rows.explainer: The rest attend awareness sessions or community trainings. 40% (20-60%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of conflict-affected people with a mental disorder

source.title: Charlson et al. (2019), New WHO prevalence estimates of mental disorders in conflict settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis, The Lancet 394:240-248
source.quote: The mean prevalence of mental disorders (depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia) was 22.1% (95% UI 18.8-25.7) at any point in time in the conflict-affected populations assessed.

rows.explainer: Used for the violence branch's survivors and women at risk, who are mostly in conflict and displacement settings.

rows.label: Effect of survivors' care and protection on distress, in SDs, for those with a disorder
rows.explainer: Psychosocial support and case management for survivors reduce distress by small to moderate amounts in humanitarian trials; the same 0.3 SD (0.1-0.5) as the site's Save the Children protection branch. Our judgment.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained per directly supported person from less violence (points a year)
rows.explainer: Community prevention programmes cut intimate partner violence in some trials (SASA! in Uganda by about half: Abramsky et al. 2014), less often in camps; a small fall in risk spread over all participants: 0.05 points (0-0.2). Our judgment.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person counted, discounted
rows.explainer: Distress relieved for those with a disorder and less violence for all directly supported, over the same years as mental-health support.

rows.label: Share of the legal count given individual assistance or representation
rows.explainer: The rest get legal information sessions. 35% (20-60%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Extra chance the help wins a person legal status or documents
rows.explainer: Regularisation drives such as Colombia's PEP and Temporary Protection Status are open to many who don't know how to apply or can't prove eligibility; legal aid helps some of them through. 10% (3-25%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Consumption gain from legal status (share)

source.title: Ibáñez, Moya, Ortega, Rozo and Urbina (2024), Life Out of the Shadows: Impacts of Amnesties in the Lives of Refugees (Joint Data Center literature review)
source.quote: Specifically, PEP led to a 48 percent increase in per capita consumption, a 22 percent increase in labor income

rows.explainer: Venezuelan migrants in Colombia granted the PEP permit against those who arrived just after the cut-off: a credible natural experiment, in the place where HIAS does much of its legal work. The published version's 48%; an earlier working paper reported 60% (IZA DP 15049), and the mechanisms (transfers, bank accounts) reach only part of those eligible: 48% (30-60%).

rows.label: Years the status gain lasts
rows.explainer: Permits run two to ten years; some would regularise later without help. 3 years (1-6). Our judgment.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person in the legal count
rows.formula: leg_direct_share * leg_status_uplift * ln(1 + status_consumption_gain) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, status_years)

rows.label: Household consumption gain from economic inclusion, a year (share)
rows.explainer: The graduation approach raised consumption by about 5-10% three years on in six countries (Banerjee et al. 2015, Science, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1260799); refugee versions, like HIAS's in Ecuador, add job placement and seed capital with mixed results. 6% (2-15%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years the consumption gain lasts
rows.explainer: Graduation gains held at seven to ten years in Bangladesh and India; refugees move more. 3 years (1-7). Our judgment.

rows.label: People in a participant's household
rows.explainer: The site's household size for Peru, standing in for Ecuador and Colombia.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per participant's household, discounted
rows.explainer: Every member of the participant's household consumes more.

rows.label: cva: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Cash and goods counted at their value; vouchers and in-kind goods are worth a little less to people than cash. 0.85 (0.7-1), as in the site's other relief models. Our judgment.

rows.label: cva: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Other agencies (UNHCR, WFP, the Red Cross) give cash in the same places, more so before the 2025 cuts. 70% (45-90%). Our judgment.

rows.label: cva: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Many HIAS programmes are UNHCR-funded partnerships where UNHCR also runs registration and logistics. 80% (60-95%). Our judgment.

rows.label: cva: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): HIAS counts the people reached, but publishes no controlled measure of what its own work did for them; the effect is from research on other programmes, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: mh: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The trials' effects come from structured programmes with trained facilitators; community-based delivery and the step from distress scales to life satisfaction add doubt. 0.6 (0.4-0.9), as for the site's Save the Children protection branch. Our judgment.

rows.label: mh: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The effect is against trials' control arms; few other services exist in eastern Chad's camps. 90% (80-100%). Our judgment.

rows.label: mh: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Partners and UNHCR co-fund some sites. 85% (70-100%). Our judgment.

rows.label: mh: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): HIAS counts the people reached, but publishes no controlled measure of what its own work did for them; the effect is from research on other programmes, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: gbv: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The effects are from trials of other programmes, the prevention evidence mixed in camps. 0.55 (0.3-0.85). Our judgment.

rows.label: gbv: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Other protection agencies cover some of the same camps and towns. 85% (70-100%). Our judgment.

rows.label: gbv: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: UNHCR and UNFPA co-fund and coordinate. 80% (60-95%). Our judgment.

rows.label: gbv: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): HIAS counts the people reached, but publishes no controlled measure of what its own work did for them; the effect is from research on other programmes, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: leg: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The consumption gain is from a credible natural experiment, but the share of clients whose status changes because of HIAS is a judgment. 0.65 (0.4-0.9). Our judgment.

rows.label: leg: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Other legal aid groups and UNHCR's own help desks would reach some. 80% (60-95%). Our judgment.

rows.label: leg: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: UNHCR funds much of the legal work and governments run the procedures. 80% (60-95%). Our judgment.

rows.label: leg: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): HIAS counts the people reached, but publishes no controlled measure of what its own work did for them; the effect is from research on other programmes, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: eco: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The graduation trials' effects transfer only partly to urban refugees. 0.65 (0.4-0.9). Our judgment.

rows.label: eco: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Some participants would find work or credit anyway. 80% (60-95%). Our judgment.

rows.label: eco: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: UNHCR has co-funded the Ecuador programme since 2017 (annual report p. 14). 80% (60-95%). Our judgment.

rows.label: eco: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): HIAS counts the people reached, but publishes no controlled measure of what its own work did for them; the effect is from research on other programmes, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Calendar-year counts stand for the fiscal year, programmes were cut mid-year after the US suspension (20 countries down to 15), and HIAS's counts are its own. 0.85 (0.7-0.95). Our judgment.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: After the 2025 cuts few funders fill the gaps a donation fills. 1 (0.9-1.05). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years from gift to spending
rows.explainer: HIAS ended the year with $4.4 million of cash against $153 million of spending (Exhibit A): money is spent within weeks. 0.15 (0.05-0.4). Our judgment.
